stops.segment: Halicarnassus, the Carian Port That Answers to the King
stops.stop: Halicarnassus, the house of Lyxes
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from one late source. The Suda, entry eta 536, confirmed verbatim at Suda On Line: 'Son of Lyxes and Dryo; of Halicarnassus... he had a brother [called] Theodoros.' The Suda is tenth-century, roughly fourteen centuries after the events. The working notes for this file gave the entry number as eta.1274, which is wrong; eta 536 is the Herodotus entry. The variant maternal name 'Rhoio' is not a manuscript variant of eta 536 at all: it comes from a different Suda entry, pi 248 on Panyassis, which names 'Rhoea, Herodotus's mother.' Both readings are recorded here and neither is preferred. The date is an ordering device only.

stops.segment: Halicarnassus, the Carian Port That Answers to the King
stops.stop: Halicarnassus, Panyassis in the house
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The kinship rests on the Suda tradition, which makes Panyassis either uncle or cousin to Herodotus and does not settle which. Panyassis's authorship of a Heracleia and an Ionica is attested in the ancient catalogues; the ranking among the canonical epic poets is a later critical judgement, not a fifth-century one. No fifth-century source connects the two men. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: Halicarnassus, the Carian Port That Answers to the King
stops.stop: Samos, the island and the dialect
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction resting on a single tenth-century source. Suda eta 536, verbatim: 'He resettled in Samos because of Lygdamis... In Samos he practised the Ionian dialect.' The subject there is Herodotus alone; the fleeing family that appears in modern summaries is an embellishment with no basis in the entry. No fifth-century source confirms exile, residence, or return. Fifth-century inscriptions from Halicarnassus itself are cut in Ionic, which undercuts the entry's own premise that the dialect had to be learned abroad. The coordinates are the Heraion of Samos at 37.67194, 26.88556 per Wikipedia; the working notes gave 37.6892, 26.8825, about 1.9 km north in the plain, and that pin has been dropped. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: Halicarnassus, the Carian Port That Answers to the King
stops.stop: Halicarnassus, Panyassis killed and the tyrant put down
stops.date_confidence: Two late claims, both from the Suda, neither confirmed by any fifth-century source. The killing is stated flatly at Suda pi 248: 'He was killed by Lygdamis, third tyrant of Halicarnassus.' The Suda gives no motive; the political opposition supplied in modern summaries is a gloss. The return, the part in the overthrow, and the second departure out of unpopularity come from eta 536 and rest on it alone. The whole episode follows the conventional biographical shape of an anti-tyrannical intellectual's life, which is a reason for caution and not a reason for rejection. Date is an ordering device; nothing dates any of it.

stops.segment: The King's Roads: Lydia, the Straits, and the Phoenician Shore
stops.stop: Sardis, the burnt temple and the Lydian kings
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the visit; the topographical detail is close enough that scholarship treats intimate knowledge of western Anatolia as probable personal experience, but no itinerary statement covers Sardis. The chapter reference in the working notes was off by one: 5.101 gives the burning of the city, the reed houses, the agora and the Pactolus, while the temple appears at 5.102, 'Sardis was then destroyed by fire, and in it also the temple of the native goddess Hybebe.' The Solon and Croesus interview is at 1.29 to 1.33 and is a set piece, not a report. Coordinates match Wikipedia's Sardis to within about 360 m. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: The King's Roads: Lydia, the Straits, and the Phoenician Shore
stops.stop: The Bosporus at Chalcedon, the sea measured in sailing days
stops.date_confidence: The measurements at Histories 4.85 to 4.86 are attested; the confident language attributed to them in the working notes is not. The text does not say 'exactly ascertained': 4.86 reads 'These measurements I have made as follows: a ship completes on an average in a long day a distance of seventy thousand fathoms,' an arithmetic estimate from sailing time, not a survey. The Macaulay text prints a dash after that colon, silently dropped in the quote field here. The Hieron does not appear in the passage at all; 4.85 puts Darius's bridge of boats in the territory of Chalcedon and puts Darius himself at the Kyanean rocks to look at the Pontus. The working notes' pin at 41.1913, 29.0898 sits between the two and matches neither, and has been dropped for Chalcedon, modern Kadikoy. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: The King's Roads: Lydia, the Straits, and the Phoenician Shore
stops.stop: Tyre, the temple of the god the Greeks call Heracles
stops.date_confidence: Attested and among the most widely accepted of his claimed destinations. Histories 2.44 presents the visit as autopsy: he says he sailed to Tyre for the purpose of the inquiry and describes the temple's two pillars, one gold and one of a stone that shone at night. The figure of some two thousand three hundred years is local priestly tradition reported as such, not verified chronology, and scholarship treats it that way. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: The King's Roads: Lydia, the Straits, and the Phoenician Shore
stops.stop: Babylon, the walls and the tower of Bel
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the most contested travel question in the whole of Herodotean scholarship. Histories 1.178 to 1.183 describes the walls, the gates, the tiered tower of Bel and the golden statue; genuine information sits beside errors of a kind a visitor should not make, and whether he ever reached the city is disputed rather than settled. This file takes no side. Coordinates are inherited byte for byte from the canonical Babylon pin already used at cyrus.journey.json, ctesias.journey.json and nabucodonosor_ii.journey.json. Date is an ordering device.

stops.segment: Egypt, from the Delta to the First Cataract
stops.stop: Naucratis, the Greek town in the Delta
stops.date_confidence: The description at Histories 2.178 to 2.179 is attested, including Amasis's grant and the cities that jointly founded the Hellenion. There is no first-person visit claim for Naucratis itself; as the standard port of entry for Greeks into Egypt a stop here is inferred rather than stated. The customs material quoted is from 2.35 and was fetched directly from the Rawlinson text. The Egyptian journey as a whole is accepted by most scholars and is conventionally placed in the 450s or 440s, but that dating has no ancient anchor and the year here is an estimate used to order the segment.

stops.segment: Egypt, from the Delta to the First Cataract
stops.stop: The Canopic mouth, the boats built like courses of brick
stops.date_confidence: The description of the Nile cargo boat, the baris, is Herodotus's own at Histories 2.96 and is attested. The pin is not: Herodotus names no town here. The coordinates are Thonis-Heracleion, the drowned port at the Canopic mouth, given by Wikipedia as 31.31278, 30.12889; the working notes' 31.3, 30.1667 sits about 3.7 km southeast and has been dropped. The pin is an editorial placement at the river mouth every Greek entering Egypt used, chosen because the hull known as Ship 17, excavated there by Franck Goddio's IEASM team between 2009 and 2011, was found to match this construction. That finding was reported in March 2019, in the Guardian of 17 March; the January 2019 date in the working notes is unsupported and no journal or month is named in the underlying citation.

stops.stop: Sais, the lake and the rites he will not describe

stops.stop: Buto, the island he watched and it did not move
stops.date_confidence: Attested at Histories 2.155 to 2.156, and among the clearest autopsy-style statements in Book 2: he describes the temple and oracle of Leto at Buto and the island of Chemmis, and states plainly that he never saw the island float or move at all. stops.stop: Giza, the pyramids and the labour figures
stops.date_confidence: Attested as text at Histories 2.124 to 2.127, and the level of description implies direct observation of the monuments; the content is another matter. stops.stop: Thebes, the wooden colossi and the generations
stops.date_confidence: The visit is attested in the itinerary sentence at Histories 2.3. The colossi episode is at 2.143, where Herodotus names Hecataeus of Miletus, the earlier Ionian prose writer, and reports the priests counting the statues against Hecataeus's claimed sixteenth-generation descent from a god. stops.segment: The Edges: Libya and the Scythian Cold
stops.stop: Cyrene, the colony and the silphium
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to any visit. Histories 4.145 to 4.205 gives the colonisation traditions, the king-list, the Libyan tribal customs and the silphium in a density of detail that makes a visit to Cyrenaica plausible; no itinerary statement confirms it, and scholarship is clear that he did not cross the Sahara or reach the remoter peoples he describes. Two mutually incompatible foundation stories, the Theran and the Cyrenaean, are set down side by side in the text without adjudication, and are left that way here. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: The Edges: Libya and the Scythian Cold
stops.stop: West of the Triton, among the Maxyans
stops.date_confidence: The passage is attested and verified verbatim at Histories 4.191 from Macaulay via Project Gutenberg 2707; the placement in the working notes was wrong twice over. The text sets this country west of the river Triton, next after the Auseans, among the Maxyans, not west of the Nasamones, who are an eastern people of the Syrtis described separately at 4.172-190. And the working coordinates of 27 N, 15 E point into the deep central Sahara, whereas Lake Tritonis is conventionally the Chott el-Djerid, which sends the description northwest toward the Tunisian Tell. The pin here is that rough correction and fixes no site: the text names none. Herodotus reports the beings as Libyan speech, with the attribution in the sentence, not as anything he saw.

stops.stop: Olbia, the king who worshipped in secret
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the visit, attested as text. The Scythian ethnography of Book 4 centres on the Greek trading zone around Olbia at the Bug and Dnieper estuary, and the Scyles episode is at 4.78 to 4.80. Scholarship judges a visit to this Greek emporion probable; a journey deep into Scythia proper is not demonstrable and is not claimed here. Archaeology of kurgan burial and horse culture corroborates much of the ethnography without touching the question of where he stood. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: The Oracles and the Battlefields of Greece
stops.stop: Dodona, the gods given their names and their shapes
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The passage is the continuation of the Dodona inquiry and is placed at that pin for that reason: Histories 2.52 has the oracle consulted about whether to adopt the divine names brought out of Egypt, and 2.53 states that Homer and Hesiod made the Greek theogony and lived four hundred years before his own time and no more. Herodotus offers the dating as his own opinion from inquiry, not as anyone's record. The same chapter is cited as attested at homer.journey.json and twice at hesiod.journey.json, where his four-hundred-year figure points to the mid-ninth century and cuts against the conventional dating of both poets. Date orders the segment.

stops.segment: The Oracles and the Battlefields of Greece
stops.stop: Delphi, the offerings in the treasuries
stops.date_confidence: Attested as description, not as declared autopsy, and the working notes had the treasury wrong. Histories 1.51 puts the golden bowl in the treasury of the people of Clazomenae and the silver one in the corner of the vestibule; it is Gyges's offerings at 1.14 that stand in the treasury the Greeks call the Corinthians', which Herodotus adds is really Kypselos's and not the Corinthian state's. There is no first-person 'I saw' at 1.51: the passage is present-tense description implying autopsy rather than asserting it, so the tag has been softened here. Coordinates inherited byte for byte from the canonical Delphi pin at cyrus.journey.json. The bribed Pythia is at 6.66.

stops.segment: The Oracles and the Battlefields of Greece
stops.stop: Olympia, the reading, or else the shade
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and two late traditions that contradict each other head on. Lucian, Herodotus or Aetion, second century CE, has him read the whole work aloud at the festival to instant Panhellenic fame; an ancient grammarian, cited without a name in the reference summaries, has him wait for cloud-shade until the audience dispersed, whence the proverb about Herodotus and his shade. Both are recorded centuries after the fact and neither is preferred here. Public performance of parts of the work is plausible on general grounds; a single-sitting recitation of nine books is not. The Muse-titles are a Hellenistic editorial arrangement, not his.

stops.segment: The Colony in the West, and Athens
stops.stop: Thurii, the new city on the plain of Sybaris
stops.date_confidence: The colony is attested: Thurii was founded in 443 under Athenian sponsorship with Pericles's backing, the colonists led out by Lampon and Xenocritus, on the plain of destroyed Sybaris in southern Italy. Herodotus's inclusion among the original colonists is ancient tradition and is tagged reconstruction, not attested. Coordinates are Wikipedia's Thurii at 39.71722, 16.49556; the working notes' 39.7075, 16.5375 sits about 4 km east, at or past the modern shoreline, and has been dropped.

stops.segment: The Colony in the West, and Athens
stops.stop: Thurii, the name in the first line
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and stronger than the working notes allowed. Aristotle's Rhetoric 3.9, at 1409a, was fetched directly from Perseus and reads: 'This is the exposition of the investigation of Herodotus of Thurii.' So a fourth-century Athenian text of the proem gave Thurii, while the manuscripts that reach Byzantium give Halicarnassus. Both readings are ancient; neither can be removed. What the variant proves about actual citizenship or permanent residence is inference, judged highly probable rather than certain. The Aristotelian citation is kept in the source apparatus and out of the narrative, per the corpus rule on later engagements.

stops.segment: The Colony in the West, and Athens
stops.stop: Athens, the verses Sophocles made
stops.date_confidence: Attested as ancient testimony, disputed as interpretation, and the date in the working notes was wrong. Plutarch, Moralia 785b, An seni respublica gerenda sit, verified verbatim at Thayer's Penelope text: 'Song for Herodotus Sophocles made when the years of his age were Five in addition to fifty.' Sophocles was born c. 497/496, so his fifty-fifth year falls in 442/441; the figure usually printed in the literature is 441/440. The 440/439 given in the working notes is one to two years late and does not follow from the age-55 datum. The poem itself does not survive. This is the strongest surviving evidence of personal contact between the two men and it does not establish a friendship.

stops.segment: The Revision, and Three Graves
stops.stop: Thurii, the second war catches up with the book
stops.date_confidence: The internal evidence is attested: passages presuppose events after 431, including early Spartan invasions of Attica and the fate of Plataea, so the text was still being worked on into the opening years of the Peloponnesian War. The finishing horizon of about 425 is a conventional scholarly estimate from the latest datable allusion, not a record of anything. The nine-book Muse division is a Hellenistic editorial arrangement and is not demonstrably his; no autograph survives and the earliest substantial papyri postdate him by centuries. The pin is Thurii for want of any evidence of where the revision happened.

stops.segment: The Revision, and Three Graves
stops.stop: Thurii, the tomb in the market place
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The tradition is confirmed verbatim in Suda eta 536: 'after he died there he was buried in the agora. But some say that he died in Pella.' The Suda, not Marcellinus, is the source for the Thurii agora tomb; Marcellinus gives the Athens version. No grave has been securely excavated or identified anywhere. The death date of about 425 is conventional and is derived from the latest datable allusion in the work, not from any record of a death. World History Encyclopedia, fetched directly, reports a rival view that he died in Athens of the plague that killed Pericles, sometime between 425 and 413; the working notes reversed that range to 429-425 and that misquotation is not carried here.

stops.segment: The Revision, and Three Graves
stops.stop: Athens, the grave beside Thucydides
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, from Marcellinus's Life of Thucydides, late antiquity, which associates Herodotus's burial with the family tomb of Thucydides at Athens. Likely a symbolic pairing of the two historians rather than a topographical claim; the coordinates approximate the Kerameikos and Melitides Gate area where such tombs were sited and identify no grave. The related anecdote of the boy Thucydides weeping at a recitation is later still, elaborated by Photius in the ninth century and Tzetzes in the twelfth on Suda-era material. Three incompatible burial traditions stand: Thurii, Pella, Athens. The multiplicity is the historical fact and this file resolves none of it.
